summary:
SMARTFARM – NASA EARTH INSIGHTS

SMARTFARM is a satellite-based agricultural monitoring application developed to help farmers understand the health of their crops and identify possible drought conditions in their fields. Designed for Karnataka, India, the application allows users to select a district and mark their farm using a rectangle or by drawing its boundary on a map.

The application analyses satellite data to calculate vegetation indices such as NDVI, EVI and NDMI, which help assess crop health and vegetation conditions. It also uses rainfall data and NASA soil-moisture observations to understand water availability and possible agricultural stress.

By bringing crop health, rainfall and soil moisture information together in one easy-to-use platform, SMARTFARM addresses the challenge of adapting agriculture to changing environmental and climatic conditions. It aims to make Earth observation data more understandable and useful for farmers, supporting better-informed decisions about crop monitoring, irrigation and water management.
details:
Project Description – SMARTFARM

What does the project do and how does it work?

SMARTFARM is an interactive web application developed using Google Earth Engine. It focuses on agricultural monitoring in Karnataka, India. Users can select a district and define their farm area either by drawing a rectangle or by creating their own farm boundary on the map.

The application has two main modules:

Module 1 – Crop Health Monitoring: It uses Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 satellite imagery to calculate three vegetation indices:

  • NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) to assess vegetation greenness and crop health.
  • EVI (Enhanced Vegetation Index) to monitor vegetation conditions.
  • NDMI (Normalized Difference Moisture Index) to understand vegetation moisture conditions.

It displays vegetation-index statistics and an NDVI time-series chart to help users observe changes over time.

Module 2 – Agricultural Drought Monitoring: It uses CHIRPS daily rainfall data to calculate rainfall during a selected period and compare it with historical rainfall. NASA SMAP data is used to assess surface and root-zone soil moisture. The application presents maps, statistics and simple interpretations to help users understand possible rainfall deficits and soil-moisture stress.

What are the benefits and intended impact?

SMARTFARM makes satellite-based agricultural information accessible through a simple, interactive interface. It can help farmers monitor changes in crop conditions, understand rainfall patterns, identify possible moisture stress and make better-informed decisions about irrigation and farm water management.

The intended impact is to promote climate-resilient and water-efficient agriculture by helping farmers use Earth observation information rather than depending only on visual observation of their fields.

Tools, coding languages and software used

  • Google Earth Engine (GEE) for satellite data access, processing and analysis.
  • JavaScript for application development and analysis functions.
  • Google Earth Engine User Interface (UI) for interactive maps, controls, charts and reports.
  • Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 imagery for vegetation-index calculations.
  • CHIRPS daily rainfall dataset for rainfall analysis.
  • NASA SMAP soil-moisture dataset for surface and root-zone soil moisture assessment.
  • FAO Global Administrative Unit Layers (GAUL) for Karnataka state and district boundaries.

What makes the project creative?

The creative aspect of SMARTFARM is the integration of three important agricultural indicators—crop health, rainfall and soil moisture—within a single interactive application. Users can define their own farm boundary and independently analyse rainfall and soil-moisture periods. The application converts complex satellite observations into maps, charts and simple explanations that are easier for farmers to understand.

Factors considered during development

The project considered ease of use, availability of satellite data, selection of suitable vegetation indices, historical comparison, cloud masking and the different spatial resolutions of satellite datasets. Since rainfall and SMAP soil-moisture products have relatively coarse spatial resolutions compared with individual farms, their results are presented as broader-area indicators rather than precise field measurements. The application is intended as a decision-support tool and not as a replacement for field observations or expert agricultural advice.
